# A word about Glenmore

I had hoped to tell everyone about Glenmore myself, and in a better way than this. Instead, some of you have heard from other people, and some have heard only part of it. That is my own fault. I put off a difficult conversation, and while I was putting it off, the news travelled without me.

So I’m writing here, on the blog Úna set up all those years ago, when the cousins in Boston and Perth and Leeds wanted to know what we were all at. It has carried plenty of birthdays and photographs and ordinary family news. There is room for something difficult here too. At least this way you will all have the same account from me, rather than a bit of it passed along on the phone.

I have agreed a sale on the house in Glenmore. The sale was agreed on 3 November, and it is due to close on **15 January 2027**.

I want to put that date plainly near the beginning. Nobody should have to hear it from somebody else again.

The buyers are Aoife and Kevin Joyce. Kevin is from Maam Cross, and they have two small children. They want to live in the house. It will be their home, not a holiday let. That mattered a great deal to me when I was deciding, though I know it does not take away the sadness of the decision for anyone else.

I am sorry I didn’t tell you properly before now. I am not sorry that I have decided to sell. Those are two different things, and I want to be honest about both.

***

The house near Oughterard was built in 1931 by Tom’s grandfather, Pádraig Mulkerrin. Most of you know that, but I want it written down here. It was the old Mulkerrin place long before I had anything to do with it. It was where Tom grew up, and there are people reading this who can remember things about it that I never knew.

I understand that selling it is not just a matter of my deciding I no longer want a house. There is family history in it. There are memories belonging to all of you, not only to me. I know that a place you don’t see every day can still be important to you. Living in Boston or Perth or Leeds does not make you care less about Glenmore.

Since Tom died in March 2024, I have been driving out every fortnight to air the house and check the pipes. It is forty minutes each way. On a fine day, with no particular trouble waiting for me, that is manageable enough. Sometimes I have been glad to go. Other days I have sat here knowing I ought to go and wished very much that I didn’t have to.

At first I thought keeping up those visits was simply what I would do. There was so much else to get through after Tom died that I wasn’t ready to make a decision about the house. I could drive out, open the windows, have a look around and come home. Then I could do it again a fortnight later. It gave me something definite to attend to when very little else felt definite.

But the visits have become harder, and the work hasn’t become less. An empty house still needs looking after. There is always something to check or something to worry about, particularly coming into winter. I have found that I can be at home in Galway and still be thinking about whether everything is all right out there.

I am seventy-one. That does not mean I am incapable of looking after myself, and I don’t want anyone reading this to start treating me as if I am. But I cannot make plans on the basis that I will always be able to do what I used to do, or that I should keep doing something merely because I have managed it so far.

***

There are practical things about the house that I need to explain, because they are part of this too.

Ó Flaithearta’s did the roof survey in September. There is work needed on the slates and the back chimney, and the quote was €38,000. There is also the damp in the back bedroom. The septic tank needs replacing to sell the house to anyone anyway.

I don’t give those details as if a list of repairs settles the whole question. It doesn’t. If this were only about a roof, there would be other conversations to have. But it isn’t only the roof. It is the roof and the damp and the tank, and the regular journeys, and the responsibility for what will need doing next.

For a long time I was looking at each job separately. I could get advice about this one, see about that one, leave another until the weather improved. Eventually I had to look at the whole of it and ask whether I was willing and able to carry on maintaining the place.

The answer is no. I have been slow to say that plainly, even to myself.

There is something else I haven’t told any of you. Last February I slipped on the step at the back door in the frost. I lay there for twenty minutes before I could get up.

I told nobody at the time. I had got myself up, and I didn’t want a fuss. I can hear how that sounds now, especially in a post where I am admitting that keeping things to myself has caused enough trouble already.

I’m telling you because it changed how I feel when I am there alone. Since the fall, I have been afraid. I watch the step. I think about how long I might be there if it happened again and I couldn’t get up. I don’t find that easy to admit, but it is true, and leaving it out would leave out an important part of why I have made this decision.

I cannot go on maintaining the house, and I no longer feel safe being there by myself. I should have said so sooner.

***

The price agreed with Aoife and Kevin was fair. It was less than the offer from the Dublin crowd in the summer, and I accepted the lower offer on purpose.

I wanted the house to be lived in. I wanted, if I could manage it, to sell it to people who intended to make their home there. The Joyces have two small children, and that helped me make up my mind.

Tom always said the house should have children in it, not be a museum. I remember him saying it, and I have thought about it often lately. I won’t pretend that gives me the right to speak for him about every part of this. He isn’t here for me to ask, and I miss being able to ask him. But I do know he said it.

There is comfort for me in knowing that a family wants to live there. I hope there will be wet coats at the door and the ordinary noise of children in the rooms. I expect there will be things about an old house that try their patience too. They are buying a home, with work to be done, and I am glad they want it.

That does not mean I will find it easy to hand over the keys in January. I don’t expect I will.

***

Tom proposed to me in the haggard behind the house in 1979. It was raining, and the cattle were watching. It wasn’t a grand setting for a proposal, but it was ours, and I wouldn’t exchange it for a better-planned occasion.

I have thought about that day a good deal while making this decision. I can still see him there. I can also remember the children learning to swim in the lake below the house, and Declan refusing to come out until his lips were blue. You could call him and call him. He was quite certain he wasn’t cold, whatever colour he had turned.

Those memories are part of why this has taken me so long. They are not things I have forgotten while considering surveys and offers and dates. I have been thinking about them all along.

There are so many years attached to Glenmore that sometimes I can hardly separate one visit from another. Then something very particular will come back to me, as clear as anything: Tom in the rain, or one of the children in the water, or a photograph that reminds me of who was there on a certain day.

For a while after Tom died, selling the house felt impossible. I could hardly bear to consider it. I thought I had enough change to live with, and I wanted Glenmore to remain where it was, with everything in it.

Over the best part of two years, I have come to realise that I can keep Tom’s memory without keeping the house. It has taken most of that time for me to believe it. I don’t expect everyone else to arrive at the same point just because I have written it here.

I will miss having the right to turn up, open the door and let myself in. I know there is a difference between remembering a place and still having it in the family. I’m not going to tell you there isn’t. But keeping it has become more than I can manage, and I cannot ignore that because I wish the circumstances were different.

***

I need to say something about Declan, and I want to do it carefully, because he reads this too.

Declan heard about the sale from his cousin Gráinne on a WhatsApp, instead of from me. He rang me at two in the morning his time. He was very upset. He said I was “selling Dad”, and I said things back that I shouldn’t have said.

I was hurt, and I answered him badly. I am sorry for that. I am also sorry that he found out through a message from somebody else. Whatever he and I might have said to each other if I had told him properly, he should have heard it from me first.

I regret not consulting him. I had been thinking about the house for so long that I failed to allow for how sudden the news would be to him. The roof survey wasn’t sudden to me. The worry wasn’t sudden to me. The decision had been taking shape over months. He was given the result without having been part of any of that, and I can understand why he felt shut out.

I should have spoken while I was still thinking, rather than waiting until I had something settled to announce. I can’t put that right now by explaining how difficult I found the conversation. I avoided it, and that made it worse.

But I also need to say that I am not willing to wait until his summer visit. The sale is due to close on 15 January, and I intend to go ahead. I don’t want to leave any uncertainty about that, or let anyone think the date is being held open while we discuss it.

Declan, I am not angry with you. I was angry on the phone, but I am not sitting here keeping it going. I know you love your dad. You don’t have to persuade me of that, and you don’t have to pretend to be happy about the house.

I would like us to talk again. We may still disagree when we do. I hope we can manage it without hurting each other as we did that night. The door is open, and there is no need to wait for a particular visit or occasion to ring me.

***

There are things from Glenmore that are staying with the family, and I want you all to know what they are.

The dresser is going to Úna’s. We are keeping Pádraig’s fiddle, the photographs, the Sacred Heart lamp and the gate sign.

I know these things will not replace the house for anyone. Still, it matters to me that they are being kept, and that you know they are not being left behind in the clearing. The photographs especially belong to the family’s story, and we will have them.

Aoife and Kevin have also said that family can come out and walk the land any time. I was very touched by that. It was generous of them, and I wanted to pass it on to you.

Of course, once the sale is complete, it will be their home, and we will need to respect that. We won’t be arriving as if we still own the place. But I am glad they understand that the family has an attachment to it, and glad they have made us welcome in that way.

There is time before January for us to be there together, too. I don’t want all our remaining visits to be about sorting things and clearing rooms.

***

We will have a family day at the house on **Sunday 13 December**, before it is cleared.

Anyone who can come is very welcome. There will be soup and sandwiches. Bring wellies, and something warm, and we can go out for a walk if the weather allows.

I know December is a difficult time to travel, especially for those of you far away. Please don’t feel you have to explain if you cannot make it. This family has been spread across enough countries for enough years that we all know wanting to be somewhere and being able to get there are different matters.

For those who can come, I would like a day together at Glenmore. You can be sad, or cross, or not know quite what to say. Nobody has to arrive having made peace with the sale. Nor does anyone have to make a speech. We can eat something, walk about and spend a bit of time in the place together before it changes hands.

Let me know if you think you’ll be there, so I have some idea of how much soup to make.

I wish I had handled the telling of this better. I wish I had picked up the phone before the news found its own way around the family. I am sorry to everyone who was hurt by hearing it second-hand, and particularly to Declan.

The decision itself has been made slowly, with a fair amount of sadness and some fear that I should have admitted before now. I believe it is the right one for me. I am glad that Aoife and Kevin and their children will live in the house, even while I am sorry that our time with it is ending.

So those are the dates, from me: Sunday 13 December for anyone who can join us, and 15 January 2027 for the closing of the sale.

I hope I’ll see as many of you as possible in December. There will be plenty of sandwiches. Bring the wellies.
